name: Azulejo
basis: why: cobalt on unfired white tin glaze, depth of blue set by paint thickness; how: cobalt ramp, tile grid, corner rosettes, crackle

lumenary.blurb: The painted tiles of Portugal and Spain: cobalt on white glaze, one square at a time. Your picture is the wash, and a rosette is painted at every corner, so four tiles together make a whole flower.

why: An azulejo painter works with cobalt oxide on an unfired white glaze of tin. The cobalt sinks in as the tile is fired and cannot be corrected, so the thickness of the paint decides how dark the blue becomes. Tiles are painted one by one so that the corner of each tile holds part of a rosette, and four tiles together make a whole flower.
how: Blur the picture twice and map it to a four-stop ramp from deep cobalt through mid blue and a pale wash to white glaze, with a streak of noise standing for the brush.
Lay tiles on a grid with a thin grout line and a small bevel lit from the top left.
Paint a pattern on every tile so that the corner of one tile holds a quarter of a rosette, completed by its three neighbours.
Add brush lines and glaze crackle.
Choose a pigment: cobalt, manganese purple or copper green.
history: The word comes from the Arabic az-zulayj, small polished stone. Portugal and Spain took up painted tiles in the sixteenth century, and the Portuguese king Manuel I is said to have admired tiles in Seville in 1503. In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries blue and white came to cover churches, palaces, stations and the fronts of houses, including the panels at São Bento station in Porto, painted by Jorge Colaço and completed in 1930.
uses: Street signs and facades in Portuguese cities
terms: A painted and glazed ceramic tile from Portugal or Spain.
An opaque white glaze made with tin oxide.
A mineral used for blue pigment.
paragraphs: The word comes from the Arabic for “small polished stone”. Spain and Portugal took up painted tiles in the sixteenth century, and in Portugal blue and white came to cover churches, stations and the fronts of houses. The painter works with cobalt oxide on an unfired glaze of tin that is white and opaque. The cobalt sinks in as the tile is fired and cannot be changed, so the thickness of the paint sets how dark the blue is. The program mimics that. The picture is blurred twice and mapped to a four-stop ramp from deep cobalt through a mid blue and a pale wash to white glaze, with a streak of noise that stands in for the brush.

Tiles are laid on a grid with a thin grout line and a small bevel that is lit from the top left. A pattern is painted on every tile in which the corner of one tile holds a quarter of a rosette, so four tiles together make a whole flower, and a small flower sits in the middle of each. The pattern is blended in the dark pigment on the light parts of the picture and in white glaze on the dark parts, so it is never lost. Edge detection adds a fine brush outline, and a Worley crackle gives the glaze its hairline cracks.

equations.note: Distances from the nearest tile corner, in tile units (u and v run 0 to 1 across the tile).
The quarter rosette. |cos 4θ| has eight lobes round a full circle, so four tiles meeting make eight petals.
The painted pattern: p is the slider, and P the pigment chosen so it always contrasts with the wash beneath.

presets.text: Manganese purple makes a rarer, older look.
Large tiles show the rosette clearly.
Heavy crackle looks like old glaze.
